Aon plc, the re/insurance broker, announced the successful renewal of the Aon Client Treaty (ACT) facility.
From Jan. 1, 2027, the facility will enable 35% co-insurance on eligible business placed through Aon’s Global Broking Centre and on facultative reinsurance placed by Aon’s Reinsurance Solutions, up from 28.5%.
Strong support from market partners has matched growing client demand for committed capacity. Where permitted by local law and regulation, and subject to eligibility, the ACT Client Dividend of 1.5% will apply to the larger 35% share.
The facility is led by QBE and backed by Lloyd’s syndicates. Lloyd’s is rated “AA-” by S&P and “A+” by AM Best. Clients who choose to use ACT access its capacity on the same terms and pricing as the lead placement and may also be eligible for the dividend. Use of ACT is subject to client agreement, and Aon manages placements in line with its conflicts of interest framework.
The expansion for 2027 is particularly significant for facultative reinsurance, which ACT has supported since late 2025. Insurers placing large or complex individual risks through Aon can now access committed capacity, subject to eligibility criteria, for a larger portion of each placement.
Since its launch in 2016, ACT has placed more than $5 billion in gross written premium. Together with Aon Digital Placement Exchange, Aon Broker Copilot and Aon Claims Copilot, ACT reflects the firm’s continued investment in broking innovation. These capabilities are designed to streamline placement and claims and enhance the client experience.
“As the risks our clients face grow more complex and interconnected, efficient access to risk capital has never been more important,” said Joe Peiser, CEO Risk Capital, Aon, in a statement. “Increasing ACT to 35% gives clients greater efficiency and confidence when placing their risks. ACT is a clear demonstration of how Aon’s integrated Risk Capital approach delivers improved outcomes for clients.”
“ACT continues to evolve with what our clients need,” said Helene Madell, CEO of Global Broking Center, Aon. “Facultative reinsurance has quickly become one of the facility’s most important areas of growth and moving to 35% allows us to build on that momentum for clients.”

From hacked supermarket fridges and a record cryptocurrency theft at Binance to an emergency over flaws in widely used web software, companies worldwide are facing a wave of cyber threats executives say AI is accelerating and making more sophisticated.
The surge is straining IT departments, with staff working overnight to patch software vulnerabilities, prompting some companies to turn to and increase investment in AI-powered security tools to help manage the workload.
A cyberattack on European supermarkets on Monday, the second in three weeks in which hackers raised refrigerator and freezer temperatures, forcing retailers to discard millions of dollars’ worth of spoiled food, underscored the urgency.
Read more: European Supermarkets Rush to Patch Vulnerabilities After Region-Wide Fridge Hack
“It’s a never-ending game of cat and mouse, with very high stakes,” said Marnie Wilking, chief security officer at travel platform Booking.com.
“We shut down one route, and before we’ve even finished rolling out the fix, the bad guys have moved on to the next,” she said, adding that hundreds of engineers at the company were now building AI-powered defense systems.
Nearly 37,000 security flaws in software or computer systems were reported in the third quarter of 2026, tripling from a year earlier, according to the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, an international registry of disclosed security flaws.
“We’re seeing events of a magnitude every week, or even every couple of days, that used to be months apart,” Markus Noga, chief technology officer of German web hosting company Ionos, which serves seven million customers, told Reuters.
Ionos said it changed its security practices after seeing a spike in vulnerabilities in July, deploying AI-based monitoring systems to scan for threats and using AI-assisted tools to install patches on its systems around the clock.
“I’m kind of limited to what a nine-to-five office hours team can do and that’s no longer good enough,” Noga said.
Cyber Threats Drive Defensive Spending
Binance, hit by hackers who stole $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency, said it would increase investment in AI-enhanced detection systems. The Port of Rotterdam is working on an AI-powered “cyber shield,” while Siemens is testing advanced AI models for defensive security.
Dutch-based grocer Ahold Delhaize, which operates the Stop & Shop and Giant Food chains in the US, was hit by two hacks in the past month. The first, in mid-October, led to more than €200 million ($225 million) in sales losses and prompted a profit warning.
In that incident, Ahold took its websites and apps offline for a week after detecting an intrusion. This week, some of its stores in Belgium and Luxembourg were among those hit by cyberattacks on refrigerators across a dozen European countries.
“We’re adjusting to a new reality,” CFO Jolanda Poots-Bijl told Reuters, adding smaller firms were particularly exposed. At the same time, AI is a defensive tool, she said.
“AI also helps us to detect and to restore in a much faster way than we were ever able to do in the past,” she added.

European airlines suffered a second wave of bomb threats on Thursday that indiscriminately targeted companies from low-cost operator Wizz Air Holdings Plc to Finnish flag carrier Finnair Oyj, throwing air travel into disarray across a region already grappling with a series of security scares.
Among the flights affected was Aer Lingus Flight EI402 headed from Dublin to Rome, which was forced to make an emergency diversion to a military airfield in northern France. Finnair said two flights headed from Helsinki to Rome and Vienna got similar threats that turned out to be false.
Other carriers targeted included LOT Polish Airlines and Wizz, which was already at the receiving end of several threats earlier in the week. In the Czech Republic, police said they received bomb threats about four planes headed to Prague, and that the aircraft were searched after they touched down. Vienna’s main airport also received a warning about four flights, public broadcaster OFR reported.
Three Ryanair Holdings Plc flights headed to Sofia in Bulgaria from Madrid, Copenhagen and London were also targeted, a spokesperson for the Bulgarian ministry of transport said. Bulgarian MiG-29 fighter jets escorted the aircraft over Bulgaria’s airspace, the defense ministry said in a statement, and one of the flights was diverted to the city of Plovdiv.
Ryanair didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
“To have this in a coordinated way, I don’t think we’ve seen this before,” Ben Smith, the chief executive officer of Air France-KLM, said on a call with journalists to discuss third-quarter earnings. “It’s unfortunate and we hope it won’t give our consumers any reason to slow down or reduce their travel plan.”
No pattern has emerged around the spate of threats this week, either with the carriers drawn in or the routes that were affected. Bomb threats are rare events and almost always end up being hoaxes or the act of copycats. On average, there are more than 30,000 flights a day in Europe’s skies.
But the unusual rise in bomb threats comes at a time of heightened geopolitical tension and freak disruptions in Europe, including repeat hacking attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions into the territory.
Getting any illegal items on board is extremely difficult given how airports are ring-fenced and passenger screenings on the ground have become ever-more sophisticated.
As a result aircraft disasters involving a bomb are exceedingly rare. Notable incidents include Pan Am Flight 103 that exploded over Lockerbie in Scotland, killing all 259 people on board, in 1988, and a Russian passenger plane that was brought down by a an explosive device on board in Egypt’s Sinai peninsula in 2015, killing all 224 people on board.
Eurocontrol, the European coordinator of air traffic across the region, said it’s monitoring the situation and working closely with airlines, airports, air navigation service providers.
In Romania, authorities at Bucharest Otopeni Airport searched Wizz Flight WMT3064 after it landed from Milan with 182 passengers on board. The airport said it’s putting its safety protocol into practice, though other flights are still operating as usual.

Storms, high winds, fire hazards and equipment failure are many of the typical risks involved with the solar power industry. For the Dagda solar farm in rural Latvia, there’s now another one: drones.
The owner of the farm, Sunly, has insured Dagda and dozens of other large parks in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland worth €600 million ($670 million) in case of any spillover from the war in Ukraine. The Tallinn-based company wanted to protect its assets and reassure its investors, who have been more careful about placing their money in the region.
“We see this as a real business risk,” said Peeter Raudsik, Sunly’s head of regulation. “Several big banks are demanding terrorism and sabotage insurance as the standard.”
From an apartment building in Romania to a parked car in Lithuania, drones from the war in Ukraine have increasingly been inflicting damage along NATO’s eastern flank this year. The heightened risk is now spawning a small, but growing area of the insurance business.
Many insurers in the region, particularly in the Baltics and Poland, have begun offering political violence or war risk cover. Incidents linked to Russia’s war in Ukraine are often followed by a spike in inquiries from businesses and homeowners nervous about protecting their property.
“We have a bit of dark humor in the insurance industry: We say that the best advertisement for insurance is a neighbor’s house on fire,” said Simonas Lisauskas, chief executive officer of Lietuvos Draudimas, the largest insurer in Lithuania. “Following events like these, we definitely observe a surge in client interest.”
Standard policies usually have a conflict exemption clause. In a high-profile case in July, the UK’s High Court decided that insurers were not liable for damages from the Nord Stream gas pipeline explosion in 2022 because they were a “consequence of war” and therefore exempt.
Critical national infrastructure — such as power plants, airports, data centers and utilities — have been among the biggest entities seeking more comprehensive cover. Then there are manufacturers, shopping centers and logistics warehouses. Additionally, homeowners, hotels, churches and educational institutions — including college Vilniaus Kolegija — have taken out policies.
Lietuvos Draudimas has signed more than 100 insurance contracts with businesses since May, said Lisauskas. One of them was Swedish telecommunications operator Telia, which last month insured its Lithuanian infrastructure, including data centers, for up to €50 million. The terms weren’t disclosed.
The Vilnius and Riga airports are also assessing new options for insurance against drones and geopolitical risks. So is a major Baltic seaport that declined to be identified publicly. A spokesperson for Riga Airport said the policy it currently holds covers risks related to terrorism and sabotage.
Customers are asking for quotes and trying to understand what kind of premium they can expect. Homes can get protection for as little as an extra annual cost of €10, but corporate premiums, which are calculated based on asset value, can reach tens of thousands of euros annually.

After losing 16 House seats and their legislative supermajority, some Republicans blamed their own unpopular agenda while others pointed to national headwinds and low turnout
State Rep. Darin Chappell of Rogersville, right, speaks Wednesday with state Rep. John Simmons of Washington and state Rep-elect Tony Lovasco of Wentzville after being selected House Majority Leader (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
After losing 16 Missouri House seats Tuesday in their worst election since Watergate, Republicans are questioning whether their own legislative agenda helped drive voters away.
Some blamed national political headwinds and low Republican turnout. Others pointed directly to a string of unpopular proposals pursued by their own party.
“We need to focus on the business of the people, and quit pursuing what I would call just personal pet projects of individual legislators, and do what people want done,” said House Speaker Pro Tem Chad Perkins of Bowling Green.
In the 99 seats contested by both parties this year and in 2024, Democrats gained more than 12 percentage points. In the seats they flipped, the margin shifted an average of 21 points in favor of the Democratic candidate.
Democrats defeated 10 incumbent Republicans on Tuesday, bringing the total of new members of both parties to 64 and ending 14 years of GOP supermajorities in the House.
On Wednesday, the diminished caucus selected state Rep. Darin Chappell of Rogersville as House majority leader for the coming session. Chappell, who has been an outspoken advocate of cutting state spending, is the uncle of popular singer Chappell Roan.
Chappell was re-elected Tuesday with 70% of the vote in the 137th District in Greene County. The margin narrowed by 15 percentage points from his 2024 election.
Chappell will lead House Republicans as they try to recapture districts lost this year and defend others — 17 Republicans won by fewer than 10 percentage points.
“We’re in a total reassessment,” Chappell said in an interview with The Independent.
House Republicans will pursue policies enhancing liberty, security and prosperity, Chappell said.
“If we need to change course on specific issues, we will,” he said. “We absolutely will.”
In the 1974 election, just a few months after the resignation of President Richard Nixon, Republicans lost 17 seats in the Missouri House. That year, as in this, Democrats benefited from a political backlash against Republicans.
But some lawmakers say Missouri Republicans added to their burdens by pushing an unpopular agenda. Every major policy initiative put before voters by Republicans since Gov. Mike Kehoe was sworn in last year has gone down to defeat.

While Democrats gained control of the House and Senate in this year’s midterm elections, the party won’t hold veto-proof margins when the new session of Congress begins in early January. That will require congressional leaders and the president to find compromise on legislation.
Failure to do so would block any bills that could improve the lives of Americans from becoming law and potentially lead to more shutdowns, since Congress must fund the government every year.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who will very likely become speaker in January, and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, will set the tone for that relationship, though committee chairs will play a significant role as well.
Trump said during an impromptu press conference Wednesday in the construction zone for his White House ballroom that he will “get along, probably, with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive. But I have the power of the veto.”

“I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did that,” he said.
‘Trump’s supplicant Senate’

“This war must end,” he said. “And make no mistake, whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court and entangle him in legislative razor wire. The days of Trump’s supplicant Senate are over.”

Missouri’s CAFO policy is built to multiply pollution, not prevent it
(Photo by Kent Becker, U.S. Geological Survey)
Missouri’s refusal to establish setback spacing requirements between concentrated animal feeding operations, to CAFOs. isn’t just a bureaucratic oversight — it’s a structural failure that guarantees cumulative pollution.
Our laws treat each CAFO as if it exists in isolation, but rural communities live with the reality of multiple industrial barns clustered together, all potentially draining into the same creeks, the same wells, and the same air column.
A single large CAFO can produce more manure than a small city. When two or three facilities operate side by side with no spacing requirements whatsoever, their waste streams can overlap. Yet the state reviews each permit separately instead of asking the obvious question: What happens when all that waste enters the same watershed? Rural Missouri already shows the consequences: increasing nitrate levels in private wells, persistent phosphorus pollution in streams, and industrial odors so strong that nearby residents cannot open their windows.
Missouri’s list of impaired waters has grown from 24 streams in 2002 to 549 in 2026. Of these, 215 were added after local control was removed in 2020 by SB391. Nearly half are impaired by e-coli or nutrients, potentially linked to CAFO waste and runoff.
The absence of setbacks is a likely accelerant. It allows industrial barns to stack like freight containers, concentrating millions of gallons of manure and wastewater in tight clusters. Regulators may insist each facility “meets its permit,” but permits don’t account for the combined load of multiple CAFOs operating in the same drainage area. Rural residents aren’t living next to one operation: they’re living next to the accumulated waste of an entire cluster.
A new trend is making the problem even worse: CAFOs are deliberately building barns just under the permit threshold to avoid regulation altogether. By staying a few animals below the number that triggers a state operation permit, operators side-step engineering reviews, public notice requirements, and even basic environmental safeguards. These “permit‑exempt” barns still produce enormous quantities of manure, yet they operate with virtually no oversight.
This loophole has become a strategy. Instead of one fully regulated barn, companies build two or three unregulated barns — each technically below the threshold but collectively producing the same waste load as a major CAFO. And because Missouri has no setbacks for Class II operations, these barns can be placed right next to each other, creating a de facto industrial complex with none of the protections that would normally apply.
The problem doesn’t stop at the property line. Missouri also refuses to regulate exported chicken litter — the waste hauled off‑site and spread on fields miles away. This creates a second layer of cumulative impact. A CAFO can legally export thousands of tons of manure into a watershed already saturated by neighboring operations, and regulators will still claim “no violation” because each facility’s paperwork looks clean.
This is the core failure: Missouri regulates CAFOs as isolated units, but pollution behaves as a single, combined system. Without setbacks, without spacing, without limits on exported waste, and without closing the permit‑exempt barn loophole, the cumulative burden grows heavier every year.

The Democratic midterm election sweep could result in changes in economic policies related to trade, spending priorities and artificial intelligence. But the biggest forces shaping the economy aren't going to change just because the party in power did.
Affordability pressures, heavy levels of government spending and growth that is dependent on the artificial-intelligence tailwind are likely to persist, economists say. And all of those factors pose risks to the economy.
"It's in a very kind of fragile place, and I don't know that it would take a lot to push the economy off the rails, and recession becomes a much greater risk," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "That isn't the case at the moment, but I don't think that's gone away."
Zandi said he had been worried before the election that the economy was under threat from inflation, an underwhelming labor market and geopolitical dangers, and remains concerned now.
Democrats romped to upset wins in not only House and Senate races but also governor and other state races. But economic and foreign policy is largely set in the executive branch, and President Donald Trump remains far apart from his Democratic adversaries, though he said Wednesday he anticipates working with them.
"I don't expect any change in economic policy. The Iran war, the tariffs and trade policy, the heavy-handed immigration policy, all are done under executive order. They're not legislatively driven," Zandi said.
"The president thought they were good policies before the election. I don't know why he'd change his mind after the election," he added. "So I think they will continue to be policies that restrain growth and add to inflationary pressures and interest rates."
Zandi sees the AI hyperscaler build-out as a key to economic growth, but also a source of potential peril.
"The risks are decidedly to the downside because the growth is so dependent on AI, and the AI growth effects are so dependent on the equity market, and the equity market is so dependent on the valuations," he said. "It just feels like kind of a very fragile place, and the labor market is not well functioning."

The Bank of England announced its first interest rate hike in over three years on Thursday, raising its key rate by 25 basis points to 4%.
The widely anticipated move marked the bank's first hike since Aug. 2023, and made it the last major central bank to embark on a tightening cycle since the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran eight months ago.
The majority of the bank's Monetary Policy Committee voted for the quarter-point hike, with the motion passing by 8 votes to 1. The dissenting member voted to raise the bank's key interest rate by 50 basis points to 4.25%.
"The conflict in the Middle East is now in its ninth month," the MPC said in a statement Thursday. "Global energy prices have continued to rise from an already elevated level."
Policymakers said they now expected U.K. inflation to rise to "about 5%" by the middle of 2027.
"It is then projected to fall as the impact of rising energy prices on 12-month inflation rates fades, and still restrictive monetary policy bears down on inflation," they said.
Ahead of the decision being announced, markets had been pricing in more than a 99% chance of a rate hike, according to LSEG data. Traders were also pricing in a one-in-four chance of a further hike in December.
Iran war intensifies inflation pressure
Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said in the November Monetary Policy Report that without "real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East... risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside."
"Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach, dependent on the evidence on energy prices and inflation dynamics," he said.
Data released earlier this month showed that the U.K.'s annual inflation rate jumped to 3.5% in September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels.
As a net energy importer, the U.K. is particularly vulnerable to external energy shocks — such as the one caused this year by the Iran war.

In his season-ending press conference, Cardinals president of baseball operations Chaim Bloom addressed several topics, from the team’s coaching staff to whether it will add pitching in the offseason to the progress of many of the team’s rookies this past season. But he created perhaps the most intrigue with his description of the team’s situation at third base, which he described as being a “long-term vacancy.”
Much of the Cardinals’ lineup looks mostly set for 2027, at least for now:
C: Leo Bernal
1B: Alec Burleson
2B: JJ Wetherholt
SS: Masyn Winn
LF: Joshua Baez
RF: Jordan Walker
DH: Ivan Herrera
That leaves center field and, yes, third base. So, with free agency now underway and the non-tender deadline looming on Nov. 20, here’s a look at five potential options for the Cardinals at third base for 2027.
The former top prospect: Nolan Gorman
This is probably the least likely name on the list. Given one more chance to win the third base job that was once thought to be his for the foreseeable future, Gorman struggled mightily in 2026, hitting .184 with just nine homers in 85 games. He was sent down to the Minors in June and stayed for two months to work on his swing, but he didn’t look appreciably better upon returning in late August, posting a .523 OPS in 73 plate appearances.
Gorman was a first-round pick by the Cardinals in 2018, and he’s been with the club for parts of five seasons, so he’s now due for a raise via arbitration in 2027. If the Cardinals can’t find a suitor willing to buy low on him, they could choose to non-tender Gorman, cutting him loose rather than offering him a contract for 2027. But the power stroke is still real, and this is a guy who had 27 homers as recently as 2023 … so maybe they give him one more chance?
The rookie: Blaze Jordan
Jordan was the player who was called up in June when Gorman was sent down, which was considered a surprise at the time because it was thought that Jordan wasn’t a good enough fielder to hold down third base on a regular basis. It turned out his defense was perfectly adequate, but the bat did not play as hoped. Jordan posted a .276 OBP, with only three homers and seven walks in 58 games.
That was a bit of a disappointment, considering he had a robust .921 OPS at Triple-A Memphis when he was called up. However, Jordan had been hitting a little better when he sustained a season-ending high ankle sprain on Aug. 27. Bloom, who drafted Jordan when he was with the Red Sox, clearly believes in him, and if Jordan is healthy, he might be the path of least resistance in the short term. But he’s going to have to hit a lot better if he wants to hold onto that job for long.
The utility guy: Thomas Saggese

The stock retreated by November 4, trading 7.6% below its close on the eve of the report. Shareholders own Exxon for profits and payouts that endure through the oil cycle, and its profit just jumped. So is that higher profit Exxon’s own, or the market’s?
Exxon’s Higher Profit Is Only Two Quarters Old
So far, more of it looks like the market’s. Exxon earned $15.4 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, against $7.55 billion a year earlier. The company earned $4.18 billion in fiscal Q1 2026, meaning the whole step up arrived in the last two quarters. Fiscal Q2 2026 profit was already $14.5 billion.
Management said a lack of supply led to tight markets and higher prices. Its guess was that fuel markets would not get back closer to normal until well through 2027, or longer. Chevron and ConocoPhillips shares rose by similar amounts on report day, so the quarter did little to set Exxon apart from its peers.
Exxon does have gains of its own. Management cited $16.9 billion of structural cost savings since 2019. Setting aside Middle East impacts, executives said production rose from a year earlier, helped by growth in the Permian and Guyana. Those savings accumulated over several years, while the higher profit has lasted just two quarters.
Payouts Are Covered By Exxon’s Cash Flow For Now
Exxon’s payouts hold up so far. The company returned $9.4 billion to holders through dividends and buybacks in fiscal Q3 2026, against $18.5 billion of free cash flow.
Management raised the dividend per share 4%, marking its 44th straight year of increases. The company also plans to keep buybacks at $20 billion in 2027, assuming reasonable market conditions. Exxon carries light debt as well, at 4.9% of its market value against 19.2% for the S&P 500.
What Happened After Exxon’s Last Profit Peak?
Profit fell by more than a third, and the payouts kept going. Exxon earned $51.9 billion in the twelve months to September 2022, and $30.0 billion in the twelve months to September 2025.

Confluent, a subsidiary of IBM, has expanded its data streaming offerings with new functions aimed at supporting AI systems with real-time business context.
The company has made its Lightning Tables feature generally available on Amazon Web Services (AWS), finalising what it calls a five-pillar Data Streaming Platform (DSP).
Access deeper industry intelligence
Experience unmatched clarity with a single platform that combines unique data, AI, and human expertise.
This step adds query functionality to the existing capabilities to stream, connect, process and govern data under a unified approach for what Confluent terms the Streamhouse architecture.
The Streamhouse is intended to address a recurring challenge: as AI agents are introduced throughout enterprises, they must often make decisions based on fragmented, asynchronously updated data from a variety of systems.
This can result in decisions being made on outdated or conflicting information, potentially disrupting workflows.
The Streamhouse aims to resolve this by enabling the continuous capture, processing, governance and provision of current business information across systems, applications and analytics tools.
Confluent has illustrated the potential use case of an airline managing flight operations, where multiple systems can offer inconsistent views of aircraft locations, schedules and seat availability.
The Streamhouse model is designed to provide a constantly updated, shared view, allowing operational teams and AI decision-makers to respond in a timely and coordinated manner.
The architecture of the Streamhouse is built around three principles: it maintains continuously updated business information, it is designed for high availability and reliability, and it operates without requiring all data to be physically consolidated beforehand.
Rather than replacing existing data warehouses and lakehouses, it adds a real-time operational layer to support decision-making and actions.
At the centre of Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform is Apache Kafka, which streams business events.
The platform includes more than 150 managed and custom connectors for integrating enterprise data, batch execution features with Apache Flink, and tools for security and data governance such as schema and access policy controls.
The new query function offers several interfaces, including Confluent Tableflow for analytics, a Real-Time Context Engine for AI agents, and Lightning Tables for rapid SQL or API-based queries.
According to the company, Lightning Tables provides a read-only serving layer for data captured in Apache Kafka, enabling queries with reported latency between 10ms and 100ms and throughput exceeding 1,000 queries per second.
Features include multiple query interfaces, unified data governance, schema management and a machine learning feature store.
IBM Confluent and data general manager Shaun Clowes said: “The next era of enterprise AI will be won by the agents that know what’s happening in the business the moment they act. That’s what a Streamhouse can deliver.
“With Lightning Tables, our Data Streaming Platform gives each agent and application a live, governed view of the business. This means companies can act on fraud signals sooner, serve customers in the moment and run operations on what’s true now versus what was true yesterday.”

So what share of Alphabet’s sales do you think goes to that bill today?
How Big Is Alphabet’s Spending Bill?
That spending consumed 33.9% of Alphabet’s sales over the last twelve months, up from 9.7% in the twelve months to September 2023. In dollars, the bill is about 5.5 times as large as it was three years ago. And it is still growing: Alphabet spent 114.4% more in the quarter to September 2026 than it did in the same quarter a year earlier.
Can Alphabet Pay For It?
Alphabet spent more on buildings and equipment than its business brought in as cash in the quarter to September 2026. In the same quarter a year earlier, that spending took only 49.5% of that cash.
Each row is one fiscal quarter. Cash left over is the cash the business brought in minus the spending (free cash flow). The spending leaves out equipment taken on through leases.
The cash left over after this spending went from a surplus to a shortfall, and it fell below zero in two of the last four quarters. Management said an inventory build for TPU system sales also held back cash in the latest quarter. Paying a 2018 fine in that quarter did as well. Even so, the business did not cover the bill on its own in the latest quarter.
Over the last twelve months, the business did still cover the bill. Spending stood at 89.0% of the cash the business brought in, but only because the quarters to December 2025 and March 2026 generated spare cash. Alphabet also ended September with $265 billion in cash and short-term investments, compared with $142 billion of debt. That cash includes $90.4 billion of stock Alphabet holds in other companies, and its debt was $33.7 billion a year earlier.

Alphabet’s twelve-month sales grew 58.5% over the three years to September 2026. The company spent $287 billion on buildings and equipment during that time, and its business now brings in $73.1 billion more cash a year than it did then.

Missouri childcare subsidy waitlist grows as providers struggle to fill classrooms
State officials aren’t requesting more money for next year and say they’ll resume processing applications only when monthly spending consistently falls below budget
Children play at Kids in Christ Academy in Kansas City with teacher Heather Malone on Oct. 23 (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).
Missouri childcare providers have classrooms sitting empty and parents eager to fill them. But with funding stretched thin, the state isn’t approving most new applications for subsidies that would make those openings affordable.
There were 11,618 children on the waiting list for Missouri’s childcare subsidy program on Oct. 5 — more than a third of all children eligible for assistance — according to the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education.
The department established the waiting list after demand increased by 19% between January 2025 and late February, exceeding the amount of money appropriated for fiscal year 2026.
No children have been moved off the list since it started March 1.
The program helps cover the cost of childcare for families earning no more than 150% of the federal poverty level. That’s $40,980 for a family of three, or the equivalent of one person earning $19.70 per hour for a year of full-time work. Families are responsible for paying a sliding scale rate based on their monthly income.
The average annual cost of childcare for an infant in Missouri is $13,780, according to Child Care Aware of Missouri. For a 4-year-old, it’s $9,568.
For families on the waiting list, that means finding a way to pay for care themselves — or going without it.
Christina Puckett, owner of Kids in Christ Academy in Kansas City, which serves 84 children ages six months through preschool, told The Independent she tries to help when she can.
Even before the waitlist, Puckett said, some families receiving subsidies struggled to pay their sliding scale rate.
“The struggle was there before the waiting list,” Puckett said.
Now families ask Puckett if they can enroll their children at Kids in Christ and pay out of pocket until the department begins processing applications on the waiting list.
Puckett said she gives discounts “just to help some parents because they can’t afford that.”
“I have them text me, ‘Can I bring my kid in? I just want to pay you,’” Puckett said. “Well, I know they can’t afford to pay me, so then what do I do?”
Despite the growing waiting list, the department is not requesting additional funding for the program in fiscal year 2028.
Its budget request of $287.6 million would maintain an increase of about $139 million in state funding included in the current budget to replace federal funding that accumulated while COVID-19 relief funds were still flowing. But it would omit $17.2 million restricted by Gov. Mike Kehoe in June in the current budget.
A statement released by the department indicated requesting additional funds “was not feasible” because of state budget constraints.
The statement said the department plans to begin processing waitlisted applications when monthly subsidy payments consistently fall below $28 million — the amount available per month in the current state budget.
The department met that benchmark in September, the most recent month with published data, spending $26.9 million on subsidy payments.

Modern life has made movement optional like never before. ASICS research found that respondents around the world reported spending 86 percent of their waking day not moving. Yet our bodies were shaped by a very different world, where walking, carrying, and running were part of everyday survival.
Around two million years ago, our ancestors began developing a body equipped for endurance running. These adaptations helped them keep moving over long distances. We inherited that capacity, but modern life gives many of us little reason to use it.
A marathon puts that evolutionary inheritance to the test, with modern training, nutrition, and technology helping runners explore their limits. So how would we perform lined up against the ancestors who helped shape us? Could a recreational marathoner outrun Homo erectus?
Evolution Toward Endurance
Unlike other mammals, “humans aren’t especially good sprinters, but we are highly effective endurance athletes,” says David Raichlen, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Southern California.
Some two million years ago, our ancestors Homo erectus lived as hunter-gatherers, spending long periods walking, tracking, and chasing food. “Around the same time, they began to develop some anatomical features that improved their ability to run for long periods,” Raichlen says. “These features include long legs, relatively short toes, long Achilles tendons, a large gluteus maximus, and other traits that help to stabilize the head and trunk while running.”
Our ability to sweat profusely may also have given early humans an advantage in hot conditions, allowing them to cool down and keep moving while other animals overheated.
One popular explanation is persistence hunting: chasing prey over hours until it collapses from heat exhaustion. Professor Lewis Halsey, of the University of Roehampton, says the evidence has become more nuanced. His own research comparing humans and horses supports a human heat-endurance advantage. Humans are less adversely affected by rising temperatures than horses, although horses remain faster. Human success, he suggests, may have come from combining a modest heat advantage with pacing, tracking, cooperation, and a large brain for tactics.
The Marathon Question
Some internet speculations suggest Homo erectus could run a marathon in around 3 to 4 hours. If the estimate were taken at face value, even its slower end would beat today’s average marathon time of around 4:30 (4:17:00 for men and 4:43:00 for women, according to Running USA’s Industry Insights report from 2023). But where did the Homo erectus marathon time come from?
It remains unclear. One study, focused on time rather than speed and published in the 2020 Journal of Human Evolution, offers a different measure of endurance: its model estimated that Homo erectus would reach a dehydration limit after 5.5-5.7 hours of persistence hunting without drinking, under the conditions examined.
Raichlen cautions against putting a time on possible speed. “I would not say that we know Homo erectus ‘could run a 3:30 marathon’,” he says. “The stronger conclusion is that around two million years ago, humans had evolved a body capable of surprisingly impressive endurance running.”
Halsey is blunter. “Inferring a marathon time from some bones is pushing it,” he says. Many adaptations associated with running are also useful for walking, and they tell us nothing about VO2 max or lactate threshold—key determinants of distance-running

JPMorgan Chase & Co. NYSE: JPM is preparing for interest rates to move in either direction, but a rapid rise poses a broader risk to the financial system, according to Charles Bristow, the bank’s head of treasury and chief investment officer.
Bristow said the bank has stress-tested its balance sheet against higher rates and does not have a single “nightmare scenario.” His greater concern is that a sudden repricing could leave other institutions unable to adjust their balance sheets quickly, undermine confidence and trigger competition for funding.
“If the move to higher rates needs to be too fast, it will have very non-linear and unpredictable outcomes,” he said.
Rates and balance-sheet strategy
Bristow said the market was pricing just over two interest-rate hikes through the end of 2027, near what he considers the lower end of a credible range. While he said market pricing was not far off on a probability-weighted basis, he remained cautious about the risk of rates moving higher.
For JPMorgan’s investment portfolio, he said the more consequential question is where the market settles on the economy’s tendency toward inflation and the Federal Reserve’s neutral rate. Medium-term rate forwards have risen to around 5% from 3% about four years ago, he said, reflecting a shift toward an environment of higher growth, investment and inflation pressure.
The bank’s approach to managing the duration of its balance sheet has not fundamentally changed, Bristow said. JPMorgan has generally avoided longer-dated investments because it believed markets had underpriced a return to a period of substantial public- and private-sector infrastructure investment. He added that current pricing makes that position harder to maintain than it was four years ago.
He also said a proposed accounting change allowing hedging of held-to-maturity securities could give the bank room, at the margin, to take more interest-rate exposure in low-credit-risk instruments within that portfolio.
Buybacks, deposits and capital rules
Asked about a decline in third-quarter share repurchases, Bristow said the bank’s sustainable dividend is its primary capital-return commitment. Beyond that, JPMorgan weighs buybacks against potential uses of capital over the medium term.
He said growth in risk-weighted assets was running at approximately a double-digit compound annual rate and that the bank was already finding organic opportunities to deploy capital. Retaining capital for future opportunities was prudent, he said, given the bank’s cost of capital and demand for financing.
On deposits, Bristow said customers have had considerable time to seek higher rates since the 2022–2023 cycle. He said JPMorgan’s balances are behaving as expected for a bank focused on operating deposits, including retail checking accounts and balances associated with payments and custody services. Procter & Gamble vs. Colgate-Palmolive: Which Dividend Stock Is Safer?
Both consumer giants beat earnings, yet their margins are moving in opposite directions as oil prices climb and a cautious U.S. shopper holds back. One dividend carries a thin balance sheet buffer, and retirees need to know which one.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Procter & Gamble (NYSE:PG | PG Price Prediction) and Colgate-Palmolive (NYSE:CL) reported eight days apart, and both beat revenue and earnings expectations. For retirees, the key question is which dividend can absorb oil-driven cost spikes, currency swings, and a hesitant U.S. shopper? The two companies answered it differently.
Shoppers Buy More P&G Products While Colgate Wins on Price
P&G posted Q1 FY2027 core EPS of $2.00, beating the $1.89 estimate. Organic sales rose 4.0%, and volume supplied 2.4 points of that gain. That points to more households buying Tide and Pampers, which is the soundest kind of growth. Pampers Amore alone is projected to exceed $100 million in first-year sales. The cost is margin: core gross margin fell 150 basis points, and management sees a $1.4 billion after-tax commodity pressure that assumes $100 Brent crude. As management put it, “The strength is real, but it won’t be a straight line.”
Colgate beat with base EPS of $0.97 against a $0.93 estimate. Pricing drove 2.0% of its 3.6% organic growth, and base gross margin expanded 90 bps to 60.3%. That margin direction runs opposite to P&G’s. North America remains a soft spot, with volume down 3.7%. CEO Noel Wallace called the U.S. fix “very much a work in progress.”
Cash Coverage Exposes a Balance Sheet Gap
P&G’s forward dividend equals roughly 62% of its $7.00 core EPS guidance midpoint. That leaves comfortable room. FY2026 free cash flow of $15.84B covers the planned $10B-plus in dividends, with buybacks absorbing most of the rest.
Colgate grew free cash flow 7%, yet shareholders’ equity fell to $288M after years of repurchases. I see that thin buffer as a real constraint. Currency adds risk too: FX lifted Latin America sales by 6.5%, but Brazil’s real has since turned against the dollar.
Investors have rewarded Colgate’s margin story anyway. Its shares are up 29.3% year to date versus 21.33% for P&G.
Oil and U.S. Market Share Will Settle This in 2027
I’m watching whether P&G’s pricing-with-innovation approach holds as greater cost pressure arrives in the back half. Management wants more than 80% of its top U.S. customers holding or growing share by year-end. For Colgate, keep an eye on the 2027 U.S. innovation cycle. Wallace already warned, “We do not see the headwinds on commodities lightening up as we exit the year.”
Why P&G’s Dividend Looks Sturdier for Retirement Income
For income-focused investors considering these names, P&G offers a higher yield, a bigger recent raise, a longer run, and cash flow that covers the payout well even with core EPS guidance flat to slightly up. Colgate fits a dividend-growth investor who can stomach emerging-market currency swings for its expanding margins and Hill’s momentum. I would rethink my view if P&G cut guidance on oil, or if Colgate’s North American volume turned positive.

The U.S. economy isn't expected to have produced much job growth in October, with employers reluctant to hire workers but also not cutting staff amid a shrinking labor force and a growing problem of long-term unemployment.
Economists are looking for a meager nonfarm payrolls gain of 59,000, a slight uptick from the 29,000 jobs produced in September, according to the Dow Jones consensus. That result would continue a pattern of sparse growth.

And immigration is now down pretty significantly, which is reducing some of that prime-age employment."
Evaluating the health of the labor market in such a climate becomes a moving target, Bachaud said.
More clues will come Friday when the Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the October nonfarm payrolls report at 8:30 a.m. ET.
"Do we have an economy where we have a lot of productivity but not as many jobs? Do we start focusing on things like wage growth? Pezzino, a personal trainer and group fitness coach, was attempting to break a Guinness World Record for the fastest marathon dressed as a savory food. Guinness still has to review the evidence before anything becomes official, but judging by the number of people who noticed her on Sunday, finding witnesses won't be a problem.

Pezzino had been competing since childhood, starting in a local running series at age 4 before moving on to cross country and track in high school and college. A federal judge rejected Delta Air Lines’ request to dismiss a lawsuit by passengers who said they paid extra money to sit in window seats, but found themselves seated next to windowless blank walls.
US District Judge Ramon Reyes in Brooklyn ruled on Wednesday that there was a reasonable dispute over whether Delta’s contract of carriage, which says the carrier “does not offer tickets or contracts to customers that guarantee particular seats,” required Delta to provide window seats to passengers who paid for them.
Reyes did not decide the lawsuit’s merits. In July, a federal judge in San Francisco rejected United Airlines’ bid to dismiss a similar lawsuit.
Delta declined to comment on Thursday, saying it does not discuss pending litigation.
Casey Olbrantz, a lawyer for the four Delta plaintiffs, called the decision “a significant precedent in establishing that, despite federal deregulation, passengers can still hold airlines accountable when they don’t get what they paid for.”
The proposed class actions were filed in August 2025 by disgruntled passengers who found themselves seated next to walls on Boeing 737, Boeing 757 and Airbus A321 planes.
According to the plaintiffs, passengers typically buy window seats to address fear of flying and motion sickness, keep children occupied, get more light, or take in the view.
They said the absence of windows next to their seats was not disclosed during the booking process. Aircraft walls sometimes align with operating components, such as air conditioning ducts.
In seeking a dismissal of the Brooklyn case, Atlanta-based Delta said the inherent nature of airline operations, including the periodic need to substitute planes with different seating arrangements, absolved it from guaranteeing seat assignments.
Both lawsuits seek millions of dollars in damages, for more than 1 million passengers per carrier.

The law, known as Assembly Bill 1709, prohibits those platforms from offering underage children “psychologically exploitative features” that could lead to compulsive use, such as providing personal recommendations and sending videos through autoplay features. It also requires the deletion of children’s accounts with those features.
In separate lawsuits on Wednesday, Google, Meta and TikTok said the law wrongly compels them to honor the state’s preferred means of presenting content to children, and substitutes the state’s judgment for that of parents. They said the law violates the US Constitution’s First Amendment’s free speech protections, as well as Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, which broadly shields online platforms from liability over user content.

The office of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who enforces the state’s laws and is the only defendant, did not immediately respond on Thursday to requests for comment.
Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law on September 10. He said children’s safety should be central to any discussion about technology, and California “will not stand by while unregulated technology puts our children at risk.”

A state ban on all intoxicating hemp products, except for beverages, begins Nov. 12
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway announces the state’s lawsuit against American Shaman in a press conference outside her office March 31, 2026 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Missouri’s crackdown on intoxicating hemp products is already underway, a week before a new state law threatens to push thousands of businesses out of the market.
Attorney General Catherine Hanaway announced four new lawsuits Wednesday against retailers accused of illegally selling marijuana disguised as hemp. That same day, a federal judge dismissed a hemp industry challenge to the law, clearing another obstacle to its Nov. 12 implementation.
Now, some hemp business owners hoped to burn their products on the steps of the Missouri Capitol on Veterans Day, one day before the new restrictions take effect. But they were denied a permit because “open flames” are prohibited on Capitol grounds.
Hanaway told The Independent in an interview Wednesday that she didn’t need to wait for the new law to go after stores selling what’s known as “THCA flower,” a product that becomes intoxicating when smoked just like marijuana. She said laboratory test results posted on the stores’ own websites show they are selling marijuana without the required state licenses.
“The bottom line is: marijuana is legal in Missouri,” Hanaway said. “Great, just comply with the law. We have so many of these shops that are selling it, and some of them very openly and notoriously claiming that they’re selling marijuana.”
Hanaway said her concern is that products sold outside Missouri’s licensed marijuana system aren’t subject to the same state testing and safety requirements, potentially exposing consumers to harmful metals or other contaminants.
The new law tasks Hanaway’s office – along with the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, the state’s cannabis regulatory agency – with enforcement. The department previously estimated that 40,000 food establishments and smoke shops and 1,800 food manufacturers could potentially be affected by a state ban on intoxicating hemp products, “but the majority of these facilities are at low-risk of requiring investigation.”
After Nov. 12, Hanaway’s office will have “more tools at our disposal” to go after law breakers.
“You’re going to see more lawsuits,” she said. “The law is stronger and easier for us to enforce.”
Under the new law, products containing more than 0.3% total THC, including THCA, generally fall outside the state’s definition of hemp. Finished hemp-derived cannabinoid products also face a limit of 0.4 milligrams of THC per container. Intoxicating products that fall under the new restrictions can be sold only through Missouri’s licensed marijuana system.
The law establishes Missouri’s first comprehensive restrictions on intoxicating hemp products. Similar bills had been debated since 2023 but failed to pass. In the absence of comparable state oversight, smoke shops have been able to sell intoxicating hemp products containing as much as 1,000 milligrams of THC outside Missouri’s licensed marijuana dispensaries.
Under existing federal law, hemp is defined largely by its concentration of delta-9 THC. Missouri’s new law, like pending federal restrictions, takes a broader approach by counting other forms of THC, including THCA.

A gunman plowed a car into a courtyard on Citibank’s sprawling Tampa business campus on Wednesday and opened fire with a rifle, killing a woman before a security guard fatally shot him, authorities said.
The Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office did not give a motive for the shooting or say whether the gunman and his lone victim knew each other.
The attack sent workers scrambling as the suspect crashed his car among outdoor tables where people were eating lunch, then started shooting, said Chief Deputy Frank Losat of the sheriff’s office. He said 3,200 people were on the campus at work during the attack.
The gunman fatally shot the woman before a security guard confronted him in a cafeteria, Losat said. The guard and the gunman exchanged fire, and the guard killed him, Losat said.
“Was there a potential for further violence? Absolutely,” Losat told a news conference. “So kudos to that security guard.”
The names of the gunman and the woman killed were not immediately released.
Losat said four other people were taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. He didn’t know whether any of them had been shot or struck by the gunman’s vehicle.
The Citibank campus in suburban Tampa includes four three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giant’s employees.
David Dzien, a Citibank vice president, told The Associated Press he was returning to work after lunch when he saw the shooter’s sedan crash through a fence about 150 yards (137 meters) away from him, followed by an “incredible clatter” that he later realized was gunfire.
People near the crashed car suddenly dispersed and others began to scream, Dzien said, as he sprinted back into the building and evacuated through a fire escape.
“I can still hear the particular type of scream,” he said, “and I’m still trying to process it, frankly.”
The attack occurred on a day when “VIPs” who don’t normally work at the complex were present for a “quarterly review,” Dzien said.
Sheriff’s deputies began arriving at the campus within a minute of the first 911 call, Losat said. The response was huge, with more than 360 deputies — many in tactical gear — rushing to the scene.
Those deputies spent 2 1/2 hours searching and clearing the building where the shootings occurred plus adjacent office buildings, Losat said.
Radio traffic on Broadcastify.com from responding officers described an exhaustive floor-by-floor search as people were found sheltering in locked rooms and closets, then carefully escorted from the buildings and parking garage.
Citigroup said in a statement that it was “aware of an incident” at the complex and was cooperating with authorities.
Employees at the Sheraton Tampa Brandon Hotel, a few hundred feet from the Citibank complex, were having a monthly employee luncheon in the hotel’s ballroom when they saw a massive flood of police vehicles headed toward the campus.
General Manager Matt Chauvin said Citibank employees ran over and told the front desk there was an active shooter.
“We at first locked the doors and, you know, went into lockdown, but the employees kept coming over,” Chauvin said.
Chauvin estimated the hotel sheltered about 300 Citibank workers. Hotel staff gave them water and lunch, and let some go into hotel rooms “to sort of decompress or make phone calls.”
“Luckily we were far enough away that they were all safe,” he said.

The U.S. economy added jobs at a much stronger-than-expected pace in October, while the unemployment rate moved lower as the labor market showed surprising strength.
Nonfarm payrolls increased by a seasonally adjusted 165,000 for the month, compared with the Dow Jones estimate for 59,000, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday.
The unemployment rate nudged down to 4.1%, compared with the forecast for 4.2%. A more encompassing measure that includes discouraged workers and those holding part-time jobs for economic reasons rose to 7.9%, up 0.3 percentage point, amid an increase of 421,000 in the civilian labor force.
In addition to the strong payroll gains for October, prior months were revised up substantially: The August figure moved to 186,000, an upward revision of 53,000, while the September count shifted to 60,000 following an upward revision of 31,000.
Payroll gains also came in better than forecast. Average hourly earnings increased 0.4% on the month and 3.1% annually, compared with respective estimates for 0.3% and 2.9%. The average workweek was unchanged at 34.4 hours.
"Today's jobs report is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown," said Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management. "Payrolls growth surprised firmly to the upside, unemployment fell back to 4.1%, and job creation remains broad-based, pointing to an economy that is still absorbing labor comfortably rather than one beginning to buckle under tighter financial conditions."
The breadth of job growth also was strong, contrary to a trend in which healthcare had accounted for the bulk of gains.
Professional and business services saw an increase of 70,000 to lead all sectors, while healthcare was next at 42,000. Other areas seeing notable growth included transportation and warehousing (25,000) and manufacturing (19,000).
"The overall picture is a labor market that is on much better footing than a year ago," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "In 2025, the economy added barely 10,000 jobs a month and basically all were in healthcare. This year hiring is averaging nearly 75,000 a month and there's a much more broad based range of opportunities."

Florida’s newly approved property-tax cut is designed to make homes more affordable. But it could also push up another punishing cost of homeownership: insurance.
Homes in the Sunshine State are already among the most costly to insure in the US because of their exposure to hurricanes, floods and other natural hazards, risks that are being compounded by climate change. Florida’s property taxes, although rising fast, are less exceptional: The mean effective rate on owner-occupied homes ranks 27th among states.
But amid a nationwide rebellion against property taxes, a ballot measure championed by Governor Ron DeSantis and passed Tuesday by Florida voters will cut them. And by so much that it is projected to strip billions of dollars from local governments, potentially squeezing fire departments, building safety offices and other services that help protect homes and reduce losses.
That could have a knock-on impact on home insurance rates. “You ostensibly are going to pay for living in a high-risk area, either as a taxpayer or as a ratepayer,” said Jesse Keenan, a professor of sustainable real estate and urban planning at Tulane University. “It’s just shifting the burden.”
The measure, Amendment 3, narrowly cleared the 60% threshold required to amend Florida’s constitution. It increases the property-tax exemption on a homeowner’s primary residence from $50,000 to $150,000 next year and up to $250,000 in 2028. School taxes are excluded.

In his post, Brandes cited Dunedin, a small city in Pinellas County, which is doing contingency planning for having fewer firefighters working per shift.
Florida Realtors, a trade association for real-estate agents, spent heavily to support the measure, promoting it as a way to ease housing costs.
